entries.title: Your morning digest can wait for last night's sleep
entries.body: The digest now has two modes. “Same time every day” is what you have today. “As soon as it’s ready” treats your time as the earliest it may send and holds the digest until last night’s sleep has actually synced, with a deadline so it never waits indefinitely. Existing digests keep their time and stay on the same-time-every-day mode; the new one is opt-in under Settings → Notifications.

entries.title: Time-correction buttons say the time they set
entries.body: The “ate earlier than you tapped” buttons on a Telegram nudge now read “19:11 · −1h” — the actual time they will store, not just an offset to work out yourself. Press one again to go further back, and the row updates to show the time now recorded rather than the moment you tapped.

entries.title: Log a practice session with its real duration and time
entries.body: A practice quick-log keeps how long the session was and when it happened instead of assuming the moment you tapped. Plus an opt-in bedtime reminder to put your wearable on, for anyone whose sleep data goes missing on the nights they forget.

entries.title: The chat answers with what it actually knows
entries.body: Ask for a recap and you get the facts behind it, with closing tallies rather than a vague summary — plus three new things you can ask it to do.

entries.title: See why a reminder didn't send
entries.body: When the notification tick declines to send something, that decision is now recorded and readable on its own operator page, so a digest that went out late or empty can be explained instead of guessed at.

entries.title: The app tells you when your digest is going out too early
entries.body: If your morning digest usually sends before last night’s sleep has finished syncing, Settings → Notifications now says so and offers the measured time in one tap — “Last night’s sleep usually lands by 07:40.” The same line rides the digest itself, so you see it without going looking. Nothing moves until you tap, and dismissing it keeps it away unless your sleep starts landing much later.

entries.title: Imported clinical documents keep the time they stated
entries.body: The C-CDA and FHIR importers used to cut every timestamp back to a bare date at the door, so a lab drawn at 14:30 was stored as “that day” and the time was gone. They now keep whatever the document actually said. A document that states a time without a timezone stores the day only rather than guessing at an hour. Re-importing a document you already have recovers the times it originally carried.

entries.title: A garbled time is refused instead of quietly becoming midnight
entries.body: A malformed clock value used to resolve to midnight on the stated date rather than failing, which could put a dose, a corrected meal time, or a fever reading at the wrong hour. It is now refused: a workout whose start time can’t be read no longer shows as in progress with an invented duration, and an unreadable fever time is left out of the return-to-school countdown rather than guessed at noon.

entries.title: Reminders land on the minute
entries.body: The notification scheduler now ticks every 5 minutes by default (was 15), and time pickers in Settings → Notifications step through the minutes your server can actually hit. A time off that grid still saves — Settings names it in a warning instead of refusing it. Operators: TICK_SECONDS in docker-notify.sh is the knob (divisors of 60 offered); the finer default costs about 3× the tick's CPU (~35s → ~105s per day).

entries.title: Practice trends live on their Wellness cards
entries.body: Each tracked practice's 26-week view — weeks in range, cadence against your declared band, session length — now sits beside its logging and history on Wellness, collapsed by default. Trends Overview returns to digest → starred grid → body census.

entries.title: The daily check-in card is content-led
entries.body: Rows appear only when they have something to say: rating first, context and reports earn their place, and a quiet one-line door covers "not feeling well?" on an ordinary day.

entries.title: Photo capture recovers from camera trouble
entries.body: A blocked, missing, or busy camera now gets a specific explanation and platform-matched recovery steps — and a device without a live camera opens the native picker in one tap.

entries.title: Phones stay tiles-only on Trends Overview
entries.body: At every range, including 1D — the full chart is one tap away on each metric's page, and empty starred tiles keep their saved slot and stay reorderable. Adding a tile is now a compact disclosure inside the grid.

entries.title: Appointments keep their time through export and re-import
entries.body: Appointments now store their day and optional clinic-local time as separate fields, fixing a silent bug where exporting and re-importing a timed appointment dropped the time. Day-only appointments remain first-class and still export as all-day calendar events.

entries.title: Food log and dose history say which time they show
entries.body: The food correction sheet now opens with "Ate at 19:40." when an eating time was recorded — or "No eating time recorded — logged at 23:40." when it wasn't — and dose history (medications, supplements, illness timeline, school-return note) marks a filing-time clock as "recorded 7:02am" instead of presenting it as when the dose was taken.

entries.title: One shared control for "when did this happen?"
entries.body: Stating an earlier PRN dose on the dashboard now uses an absolute time with a one-tap Now — the drifting "30 min ago / 1 hr ago" chips are gone. The same control rolls out to food, dose, and measurement corrections next.

entries.title: Cycling gets its own analysis home
entries.body: Ride detail pages with charts, routes, heart-rate zones, laps, and segment efforts from Strava — plus overview trends and comparisons across road, gravel, mountain, e-bike, virtual, and indoor rides.

entries.title: Email joins the reminder channels
entries.body: Email now delivers reminders alongside Telegram, Web Push, and Home Assistant. Opt in per person under Settings → Notifications; by default emails are content-free (“something needs your attention”) so no health details reach your inbox, and you can opt your own account into full content with the trade-off stated.

entries.title: Track a full year
entries.body: The Trends and Timeline quick ranges gain a 1Y pill, rolling summaries add a 365-day window, and long-range charts plot weekly or monthly averages with a low–high band instead of an unreadable point-per-day trace.

entries.title: Reminder times are minute-precise
entries.body: Set any reminder time, not just on-the-hour. The Docker scheduler now runs every 15 minutes, and Settings warns if your server’s schedule can’t honor a sub-hourly time.

entries.title: Ride-history backfills survive anything
entries.body: Strava detail backfills run as durable jobs with live progress and an ETA on the provider page. They pause at provider rate limits and resume automatically — across navigation, restarts, and quota windows.

entries.title: Data tables behave the same everywhere
entries.body: One shared responsive shell means every records list stacks into readable cards on phones, sortable headers look alike across the app, row actions live in one consistent menu, and history lists share the same expand, edit, and undo-delete behavior.

entries.title: Reload can no longer strand the tab
entries.body: Tapping Reload on the update bar completes even when the update activates slowly — no more hung tab waiting on a swap that already happened.

entries.title: Deletion now means deletion — and undo where it counts
entries.body: Deleting a profile removes every trace of that person’s data, including nested clinical history. Bulk deletes on Data → Manage offer the same Undo toast as row deletes, and dose schedule history and record revisions now ship in exports.

entries.title: Access-control hardening
entries.body: Re-pointing a portal patient mapping now requires write access to both profiles involved, sync reports can no longer write another household login’s portal state, and undoing a delete is authorized against the profile that owns the deleted row.

entries.title: Stale taps can no longer corrupt medication state
entries.body: A double-tapped suggestion mints one medication, Pause/Resume tells you when the state already changed instead of silently inverting it, stop and restart honestly refuse when nothing changed, and a dose removed by mistake can now be restored to the schedule with its history intact.

entries.title: Every one-tap answer is honest now
entries.body: Confirming a dose from the household card, the dashboard, or Upcoming reports what actually happened — a paused item or retired dose says so instead of silently doing nothing. Marking a care-plan item done can no longer overwrite a cancellation, goal menu actions refuse stale taps, and routine and situation switches are guarded the same way.

entries.title: Health summaries say what they actually know
entries.body: Three surfaces stopped overstating their data. The Longevity biomarker pillar now says how many markers its ratio covers and how current they are — results past their retest window are named, and a panel with only old results goes neutral instead of green. The Fitness check counts tests with a current value separately from tests with any value, each test on its own clock (a month-old resting heart rate is old; a month-old strength test isn't), and the domain bars say they show your best result, with the spread. And injuries can now be declared at the level you mean — a movement, specific lifts, a side — so one sore press no longer removes every chest suggestion; the recovery easing percentage is your setting when you declare one, and the app's 60% is named as an adjustable default when you don't.

entries.title: App updates no longer eat mid-workout edits
entries.body: If the app updates while you're mid-workout, your edits are no longer lost: the editor tells you an update landed, keeps your entry safely on your device, and offers it back after one tap to reload. Quick-log taps made in that state are saved and delivered automatically once the page is fresh.

entries.title: The update bar stops re-offering what you already have
entries.body: After an update, refreshing the page really does take it now — the "Update ready" bar no longer reappears on the very page that just loaded the new version. It only shows when there is genuinely a newer build than the one you're on.

entries.title: Sleep mornings, told honestly
entries.body: Two fixes from one investigation. Fitbit Takeout nights were stored as the watch's bare clock reading, so what time you “woke up” could shift by hours depending on the server — imported nights are now pinned to the real moment in your own timezone, and already-imported nights are corrected in place (hand-edited nights are left alone). And the morning gap before your tracker delivers is now named: instead of showing a big number for an older night, the sleep card and page say “Waiting for last night's sleep” — with an arrival estimate once your own rhythm is known — then step aside the moment the night lands.

entries.title: The morning digest waits for your sleep
entries.body: An automatic digest hour now schedules itself for after your tracker actually delivers the night — measured from your own history — and if last night still hasn't arrived at send time, the digest holds for one more hour before sending either way. No more sleep section missing at random.

entries.title: Provider clock errors, fixed once at the door
entries.body: A workout arriving with a wrong time-zone offset used to be repaired symptom by symptom. Now one rule at import decides: when the true time is known, the session is filed correctly on arrival — even across midnight, even in half-hour zones like India's or Newfoundland's — and when only two disagreeing clocks exist, the pair is surfaced in Data → Review with the difference named, never guessed. The trends chart and the table beneath it also now always agree on how many readings a day has.

entries.title: "Take with food" now knows about the food
entries.body: A reminder for a with-food dose now says whether food has been logged — "food logged 20 minutes ago" or "no food logged yet" — as information beside the reminder, never a gate on it. And on the web food bar, new Now / Earlier… chips let you state when you actually ate as you log it, working offline too.

entries.title: "Last night" now means last night
entries.body: The sleep tile's freshness label was permanently one night late: the night you just woke from could never be called "Last night", and a two-night-old session wore that label every morning before your tracker synced. The naming is fixed everywhere — and sleep coaching no longer describes a stale night as last night.

entries.title: Deleted items get a home
entries.body: Everything you delete now lands in a Trash section under Data, listed with what it was and when it went — and Restore is one click, performing exactly the same restore the 15-second Undo toast always did. Items can be purged individually or all at once, and admins choose how long the Trash keeps things (30 days by default).

entries.title: Half-hour time zones, honest workout targets, a form that remembers
entries.body: Duplicate workouts from providers reporting in half-hour or 45-minute time zones (India, Newfoundland, Nepal) are now caught like their whole-hour cousins. A sport-type training target can no longer quietly mis-aim the workout suggestion at something a lift slate can't close. And the measurements form now remembers which group you last used even when the entry was logged offline.

entries.title: The protein entry sits where it ranks
entries.body: When a protocol button opened the food bar pinned to a specific group, the protein entry could render below rows it actually outranked. It now sits exactly where its ranking earns, pin or no pin.

entries.title: Sync history reads as days, not a wall of rows
entries.body: A source that syncs seventy times a day used to produce seventy identical history rows. The history now groups by day — notable runs (errors, imports, truncations) itemized, routine ones folded into an openable range — and the drill-in counts only what it can actually list, naming the remainder instead of guessing. Sync pages are also centred like the rest of the app. Under the hood, every pulled provider now runs through one shared sync engine, so each safety rule is enforced once for all of them.

entries.title: One tap means one log
entries.body: Every one-tap logging button now guards against the accidental double-tap: a brief cooldown after each success, keyed to the exact write so skip-then-unskip and similar corrections stay instant. The two taps that genuinely expect an interval — practice sessions and refills — ask a gentle "log another?" before repeating, with the refill window sized from your own supply. The practice button also shows today's live count instead of one frozen when the page loaded.

entries.title: The self-correcting digest gets cheaper and tougher
entries.body: The morning digest's self-correction now checks a cheap "did anything change?" stamp before rebuilding, so the hourly sweep does almost no work on a quiet day while your resolving act still updates the chat within the hour. And one profile's failure can no longer stall everyone else's message corrections — each is isolated.

entries.title: Belt-and-braces on dose corrections
entries.body: The in-chat dose-time correction now re-checks profile ownership at the exact moment it writes — it was safe before, but only by the grace of a neighboring query, and a new automated scan keeps every ledger write honest from now on. The dose schedule-history read that runs every hour is also cached briefly, keeping reminder ticks fast without ever judging a day by the wrong rule.

entries.title: Logging-only tabs stop signing you out early
entries.body: A tab used purely for logging — never navigating — used to let its sign-in cookie quietly expire weeks before the server would have ended the session. The cookie now stays in step with the server. Also: when an edit shrinks a day's alcohol tally, the earliest drinks are removed from the record rather than the latest, keeping "last drink at" accurate.

entries.title: Weekly counts stop at today
entries.body: A workout accidentally logged with a future date could quietly mark this week's training target as met — silencing its reminder — or inflate a substance cap. Weekly counts now stop at today on every surface, and the Fitness trends window no longer includes days that haven't happened.

entries.title: The web dose checkbox stops pretending
entries.body: Marking a dose from the web now refuses the same cases the chat and offline paths always refused — a paused medication can no longer be logged (and have a unit of supply deducted) by a stale browser tab, and the checkbox reports why instead of acting as if the write landed. Deleting a wellness practice session or a single food serving now offers Undo, like other deletions — and removing one serving of three leaves the other two alone.

entries.title: Correct a clinic reading right on the chart that shows it
entries.body: A clinic-measured reading folded onto a device metric's chart — a visit's resting heart rate beside your watch's — can now be corrected or deleted right there, instead of being chartable but untouchable. Underneath, new readings route to the right store by what they measure, and clinical provenance (which document, which visit) is always preserved.

entries.title: A wrong time zone stops doubling your workout
entries.body: When two sources record the same workout but one reports it against the wrong UTC offset, the copies used to land an hour apart and count as two activities, doubling the day's totals. Pairs a whole hour apart that agree on duration and distance now surface in Data → Review with the clock difference named — and nothing merges automatically; you choose which copy to keep.

entries.title: Your food log meets your medication's own guidance
entries.body: Log a drink during a treatment whose label says "avoid alcohol" and Allos now notices: a calm note appears on Upcoming naming what you logged and what the label says — never a push notification, never a judgment. Only interactions the data can honestly support will fire; the rest decline with a written reason rather than guessing. Food-group ranking is also now one computation, so the web bar and the Telegram keyboard order groups identically, and the protein entry ranks on the web too.

entries.title: Tell the chat when you actually ate or took it
entries.body: A Telegram food or dose tap now records when the thing actually happened, not just when you tapped. Tapped late? For about an hour afterward, one-tap chips (−1h, −2h, −3h — or an exact hour) correct the time right in the chat, and a whole late-logged meal or bedtime handful corrects together. Meal slots are no longer guessed from the clock, and a dose correction only ever moves the time earlier, so redose safety timing never loosens.

entries.title: The morning digest fixes itself
entries.body: The digest is a report, and reports can go stale: “8/9 taken — missed Glycine” used to sit in your chat all day after you logged that Glycine in the app. Now the delivered message quietly updates to match what actually happened, and only when something really changed. The digest’s workout preview also names the same workout the workout reminder suggests, sync problems explain why they matter to you, new-document lines say what was found and where, and lines that need a person to act are marked apart from the purely informational ones.

entries.title: Setting up a portal is not “overdue”
entries.body: A household that had added a patient portal but never run the companion tool used to be nagged that a routine check was overdue — contradicting the setup checklist on the very page the nudge linked to. Sync reminders now stay silent until the tool has actually reported in once. A new portal card also explains when a second login is worth adding, and warns that the choice is best made before the first run, which writes each login’s name into the tool’s configuration for good.

entries.title: Family chats stop trading buttons
entries.body: In a chat shared by a family, one person’s Telegram command could strip another person’s live buttons — the app guessed whose message each reply was and guessed the same way every time. Every message now declares who it is about, so your reminder’s buttons are yours until you use them. Command replies also got faster in busy households.

entries.title: Log measurements, on any screen, in three calm groups
entries.body: The measurements form used to decide its layout from the window instead of the space it actually had, cramming four columns into a narrow sheet. It now lays out by the room available and gathers fields into three groups — Vitals, Body, Sleep & recovery — with units shown inside each field. The Active-protocols dashboard widget now reads “On pace” exactly when every other surface does, instead of shouting “Behind” mid-week. And photographing a paper document is a proper button next to file upload on a phone, not a stray form row.

entries.title: Editing a dose stops erasing its history
entries.body: Changing a dose’s time or days used to quietly void all the adherence history from before the edit — the record was protected by throwing it away. The schedule now keeps a dated history, so each past day is judged by the rule that was actually in force then. A dose moved into the bedtime slot no longer claims earlier nights it was really an evening dose. Operator note: a schema migration applies automatically on next start.

entries.title: The workout nudge names every session it owes you
entries.body: On a day you were behind on both strength and cardio, the reminder used to suggest only the strength half while pointing its “← today” marker at the cardio target it never mentioned. Both sessions are named now, and the marker points at what the message actually suggests. Wellness practices and food targets no longer appear in the workout list as deficits a workout cannot close — practices keep their own reminder. And when weather parks an outdoor activity, the nudge says so and names the indoor stand-in, as the dashboard always did.

entries.title: Last night’s supplements can still be confirmed this morning
entries.body: The buttons under a bedtime reminder in Telegram used to vanish at midnight, though the app itself was happy to accept the confirmation for two more days. A dose’s buttons now live exactly as long as the app would honor the tap, missed-dose escalations keep theirs overnight, and only genuinely day-bound messages — like the food nudge — still close at the day boundary. A message whose window has truly run out now says where to log instead of just calling itself yesterday’s.

entries.title: A reading entered twice counts once
entries.body: A measurement recorded by hand in two places — as a body measurement and inside a medical record — used to appear twice in trend series, skewing every average drawn over it. The two stores spelled “you typed it” differently, and the chart believed both. Series now recognize one reading however it was filed. Two devices agreeing on the same value for the same day also chart once; which device said what remains visible where sources are compared.

entries.title: Your resting heart rate is finally judged against something
entries.body: A resting heart rate from a watch or scale used to be charted with nothing to compare it to — the healthy ranges lived on a different page, reachable only if you had imported a clinic document. Now the range finds the reading wherever it came from, so a trend says whether it is where it should be. This matters most for children, whose normal range is far higher than an adult’s: a three-year-old at 120 is ordinary, and the app now knows that. Readings from a clinic visit also join the same chart as the ones your device records, marked as coming from a visit.

entries.title: A record you earn again gets celebrated again
entries.body: Dismissing a personal-record note used to silence more than you meant. Because the reminder was filed under the exercise’s written name, a lift you log under two spellings counted as two separate things, and renaming or deleting old sessions could quietly move the label — so a genuinely new record sometimes arrived already hushed. Records are now tracked by the movement itself, dismissals you have already made still apply, and notes left behind by deleted history are cleared away. A few dismissed items in “Snoozed & dismissed” that used to read “no longer applies” now say what they actually were.

entries.title: Blood pressure reads as a trend, not as a lab result
entries.body: Blood pressure, oxygen saturation, breathing rate and body temperature now open on the surface built for things measured continuously — charted over time — instead of the page meant for lab results that arrive a few times a year. Children’s blood-pressure percentiles and the link to the rest of a panel came with the move. Lab values and readings like vision and hearing stay where they were, because a reference range is the right way to read them.

entries.title: Old chat buttons stop lingering
entries.body: A food reminder in Telegram sometimes left an earlier message’s buttons still live. Tapping one logged against the day it was sent rather than today, which is rarely what anyone means. Each reminder now reliably retires the one before it.

entries.title: Rain no longer reports itself in degrees
entries.body: When the weather parks an activity, the reason now reads in the unit it actually measures. A ride held back by rain used to announce “Too wet for cycling (45°C)” — millimetres of rainfall printed as a temperature. Wet days now describe themselves in plain language instead, like “heavy rain in the morning,” and temperature reasons follow the scale you have chosen rather than always showing Celsius. Days already cached before this update describe how wet it was but not when, until the next weather sync fills that in.

entries.title: A night stops vanishing from your sleep history
entries.body: If you recorded a bedtime supplement for a past night and later edited that supplement — even just fixing its name or amount — the whole night disappeared from the Sleep page, reading as though nothing had been due rather than showing what you took. What you logged is a record of that night, and editing the entry afterwards no longer erases it. Nights you never logged are unaffected and still read from your current schedule.

entries.title: The last streak is gone from Practices
entries.body:
The "N-week streak" under each practice on Trends has been retired, finishing the removal that took the training and supplement streaks earlier. It counted unbroken weeks, so one week away — ill, travelling, or simply busy — reset a real habit to zero.

What stays is the figure that was already beside it and describes you more fairly: how many of your completed weeks met the floor you set, as in "Floor met in 3 of 4 completed weeks". Everything else on the card is untouched — the week-by-week strip, the cadence chart, your frequency targets and the session-length history are all unchanged.

entries.title: Remove the exact serving you meant, not whichever one was logged last
entries.body:
The food log's ⋯ menu now offers "Remove this serving" beside "Correct this serving", so you can take out the one you are pointing at. The quick minus button beside each food is unchanged — it still removes the most recent serving of that food from the meal, which is what you want when you have just tapped one too many.

The two now agree about what a serving is. Before, if you had moved a serving into a meal and then wanted it gone, the minus button could take a different one instead, because it goes by when a serving was first tapped rather than by which one you had just been working with.

entries.title: The weight you type into a set is the weight you get
entries.body:
When you logged a set for a lift you have history for, the first set's weight and reps filled themselves in with the coached suggestion the moment your cursor arrived in the field — before you had typed anything. If you were entering your own numbers, yours landed on top of the suggested ones instead of replacing them: meaning to log 60 kg gave you 77.560, or 77.605 depending on where in the field you had tapped. Both look like real loads, so a set could be saved wrong without anything looking amiss.

Those fields now stay empty until you type in them, and what you type is the whole value. The coached suggestion has not gone anywhere: it is still previewed in grey inside the set, and the "Next set" card above still has its "Use" button, which fills weight and reps in one tap. The one change to that path is that taking the suggestion is now that tap, rather than something that happened by itself when you moved into the field.

If you have a saved set whose load looks oddly long — a suggested weight with your own digits buried in it — that is where it came from, and it is worth correcting.

entries.title: Tapping a sidebar link shows you it worked
entries.body:
Opening a section from the sidebar used to give no sign that anything had happened — the old page just sat there for a second or so while the new one was prepared out of sight. It looked frozen, so the natural response was to tap again, and that made it worse: every tap threw away the page being prepared and started over, so a link tapped impatiently could take much longer to open, or not open at all.

Now the row you tapped shows a spinner straight away and keeps it until the new page is on screen, and tapping the same row again while it is loading does nothing rather than starting over. Opening a link in a new tab or window with a modifier key works exactly as before.

entries.title: A finished import no longer wipes the form you are typing
entries.body: When an import or a document extraction finished in the background, the page refreshed itself — and if you were part-way through writing up a visit, the form went blank under you. The notification that the job finished still arrives the moment it does; only the page refresh now waits until you have saved or cleared what you were writing. The one trade is small and deliberate: while a form holds unsaved text, the list behind it catches up a few seconds later than the notification says it did.

entries.title: Streaks are gone — the numbers that survive are the ones that describe you fairly
entries.body:
The day-count streaks are retired: the one on your weekly recap, the 🔥 beside each supplement, the "N-day streak" on the training surfaces, and the badges awarded for keeping a run going. They measured how unbroken your logging was rather than how you were doing, and they had a cliff — one paused item, one illness, one deliberate skip, one trip, and the number went to zero as though the effort before it had not happened.

What replaces them is what was already there and more honest: days active, and your adherence percentage. The weekly recap also drops the lines that never earned week-scale framing. One streak is deliberately kept and you will still see it — the coaching nudge that notices you have trained several days in a row and suggests a rest day. That one exists to tell you to stop, not to keep going.

entries.title: Fix a serving logged to the wrong meal, or a photo tagged with the wrong pose
entries.body: Things you log with a single tap could only be created or deleted, never corrected — and deleting and re-logging is not the same, because a re-log lands at the current time and meal. A serving can now be moved to the right food, day or meal from the food log's ⋯ menu, and the day's counts follow it across rather than counting it twice. Progress photos can have their date, pose and caption fixed in place; the picture itself is never touched, so a correction no longer costs you the original file or its place in a comparison.

entries.title: Correct a dose you logged wrong — supplements too, not just medications
entries.body: Backfilling a dose you forgot to tick, fixing the time or amount on one you logged wrong, and removing a mis-tap with an undo now work for supplements exactly as they do for medications, from the same ⋯ menu on the dose history. Scheduled medication doses became correctable too — previously only as-needed ones were. Stock counts follow along: removing a logged dose puts the unit back in the bottle, including a bottle shared across the household. Correcting a dose from days ago will never resurrect a missed-dose reminder for that day.

entries.title: The dashboard leads with the cards you can act on
entries.body: Latest vitals and Cycle phase now sit with the cards that offer you something to do, rather than among the read-only summaries — both carry a logging action once they have data, so they belong there. A dashboard you have already arranged yourself is untouched; this changes only the order you start from.

entries.title: Seven-day averages now cover seven days — and your first reading shows up the day you take it
entries.body:
Two summary numbers disagreed about what a week meant. The Nutrition card's "7-day average" was really an average of this week so far — on a Tuesday it covered two days, it reset every Monday, and it was dragged down all afternoon by a day you had not finished eating. It is now a genuine average of the last seven complete days, and the gauge's "Avg" marker says "This week" so the two numbers no longer look like the same one.

The day you record a first-ever weight or reading, the rolling summary used to say "No readings" — exactly when you were checking whether the entry had worked. It now shows that reading, labelled as today's rather than dressed up as an average. A profile that simply has not logged in a few weeks still reads as empty, because an old number is not a recent average.

entries.title: The dashboard opens with the cards you can act on
entries.body: A fresh dashboard now leads with the cards that offer you something to do — log a dose, record a reading, start a session — and puts the read-only summaries behind them. Cards that only display a number no longer sit above the ones waiting on a tap. A dashboard you have already arranged yourself is left exactly as you arranged it; this changes only the order you start from.

entries.title: Log a cycle day from the dashboard or the quick-log sheet
entries.body: Cycle logging is now reachable from the dashboard card and from the quick-log sheet, not only from the cycles page. The phase card also stops going quiet at the moment logging matters most: when a period is due or already running, it shows the log affordance rather than hiding until the data catches up.

entries.title: Rearranging dashboard cards on a phone
entries.body: Dragging a dashboard card on a phone no longer resizes it mid-drag or leaves the dragged copy intercepting taps, and the reorder rows are compact enough to see several at once on a small screen. Saving a new arrangement now reliably takes the first tap.

entries.title: Background updates wait while you are part-way through a form
entries.body: The app repaints itself in the background when things finish elsewhere — the offline queue syncing, an import completing, a document finishing extraction. Those repaints now hold off while you have unsaved text in a record form, and land as soon as you save or clear it, so a half-filled form is not disturbed under you. Repaints you ask for yourself are unaffected: pulling to refresh still refreshes immediately, because that is the whole point of the gesture.

entries.title: Tapping "Start workout" during a workout no longer restarts its clock
entries.body: With a workout running and minimised to the dock, every entry point still said "Start workout" — and tapping one silently reset that session's elapsed time and cleared what it held. Those entry points now read "Resume workout" while a session is live and reopen the one you were in, with its clock untouched. Refills also gained a small note saying when you just refilled, so an accidental double-tap is visible rather than silently adding a second bottle; it tells you, it does not stop you, because restocking two at once is a real thing to do.

entries.title: Goals can target a lab value or a vital
entries.body: Goals could only track weight, body fat and resting heart rate, so "LDL under 100 by June" had nowhere to live and sat as plain text beside the very chart that could have answered it. A goal can now name a biomarker with a target and a direction, and its progress reads the same series the trends pages draw. Pacing works per result rather than per day — a lab goal advances when a result arrives, not on a calendar, so it will not tell you that you are behind on a day nothing was measured.

entries.title: Refreshing clears the update bar, and a stale tab recovers itself instead of showing a broken light card
entries.body: With "Update ready" showing, refreshing the page did not make it go away — the refresh fetched the new build, but the update it was offering stayed pending, so the bar returned offering an update the page was already running. A refresh now takes the waiting update when the page is already on that build, silently and with no second reload. Separately, navigating to a page a stale tab had not visited yet could land on an error card that was hard-coded light — in dark mode it read as the app breaking — and whose "Try again" could never work, because retrying reruns the same stale code. That case now reloads onto the current build automatically, at most once, and the card behind it follows your theme and offers a reload that actually fixes it.

entries.title: Two "7-day averages" that disagreed now agree, and period averages stop counting a half-finished today
entries.body: The dashboard and the metric detail page both showed a "7-day average" and could show different numbers for the same metric on the same day, because one excluded today and the other included it. They now compute the same way. The detail page's 7-, 30- and 90-day averages also stop including today: for anything that accumulates through the day, such as steps, the average was dragged down every afternoon by a day that was not over and quietly corrected itself at midnight. Averages now cover complete days only, the latest reading still shows today's value, and the labels say which is which — "vs prior 7 days" and "through yesterday".

entries.title: Hearing gets a home, and the ototoxic warning finally says what it is warning about
entries.body: Audiograms had nowhere to live: the analytes and reference ranges were already curated, but there was no way to enter a hearing test. Records → Specialty now has a Hearing pane beside Vision, storing each ear-and-frequency threshold alongside every other reading so it trends, flags and exports like the rest. Retesting a single frequency now updates only that frequency instead of blanking the others. The medication warning for hearing-toxic drugs also changed: where it used to say only that you were on one, it can now cite your own audiogram — "a documented threshold shift since January: 15 dB across 4 and 8 kHz, right ear". With no audiogram on file it says nothing extra rather than prompting you for a test you never had.

entries.title: Biomarker pickers put what matters to you first
entries.body: Every biomarker picker — starring a trend, choosing what to compare, naming a result, mapping an import — was a flat alphabetical list of roughly two hundred analytes, so the one you actually track sat wherever the alphabet put it. Opening a picker now leads with anything due for a retest or currently flagged, then the standard metrics, then the markers you have recorded before, then everything else; typing still searches the whole list. All four pickers use the same control and the same order, so moving between them does not mean relearning where things are.

entries.title: A left knee is no longer the same as a right one, and an adopted parent no longer counts as inherited risk
entries.body: Conditions can now record which side they affect, how severe they are, and their stage, and family history can record age and cause of death plus whether a relative is biological, half, adopted or step. Both were previously impossible to state and were dropped on import even when the source document said so. Two things change beyond the record itself: a left-knee and a right-knee diagnosis no longer collapse into one row on the problem list, and screening cadence now skips a relative you have marked non-biological instead of weighing their history as inherited. A biological relative's stated cause of death also counts toward that cadence — "father, heart attack at 52" previously sat in a field nothing read.

entries.title: Notification settings stop asking the same question twice
entries.body: The Home Assistant card listed all thirteen reminder kinds and so did the routing matrix's Home Assistant column — twenty-six checkboxes for thirteen choices. The card now keeps the connection settings and the matrix is the one editor. Each channel column also gains a select-all in its header, so switching a whole channel off is one tap instead of thirteen — except your dose reminders, missed-dose escalations, and redose notices, which keep their own boxes so a safety reminder can never be silenced by a single undifferentiated tap.

entries.title: Secrets stay masked in the console too, and busy logs stop losing lines
entries.body: Values that look like credentials were already masked before being written to the log files, but the copy echoed to the container console was not — the audience most likely to have the log in front of them saw the unmasked version. Both destinations now pass through the same masking step. Separately, the log files trimmed themselves by rewriting the whole file, which could silently drop an entry written by the notification service at the same moment; trimming is now safe against a second writer.

entries.title: Undoing a merge of several activities no longer loses one of them
entries.body: When a merge of three or more activities was undone, each restore ran independently — so if one failed, the surviving activity's data could end up unreachable: not on the restored rows, and no longer on the kept one. Undo now removes exactly the contribution of the activity being restored, leaving the rest intact, and retrying the failed one finishes the job.

entries.title: A brief Telegram outage no longer strands a message with stale buttons
entries.body: When the app updates a Telegram message and Telegram is briefly unreachable, it used to forget that message permanently — leaving buttons on screen that no longer did anything and could never be corrected. It now tells a temporary failure apart from a genuinely dead message, and retries the temporary ones on the next check.

entries.title: Patient portals shows the actual structure: portal, login, patient
entries.body: The portals page is now built from the objects it manages — each portal a permanent section, its logins inside it, and the patients under the login they arrived on. Mapping a patient means tapping a family member's face rather than picking from a dropdown, and when the same person shows up on two logins the page offers the match instead of looking like a duplicate. Portal names, logins, and software tags are editable in place, and changing which profile a patient maps to is a single atomic switch. Members now only see the logins covering profiles they can reach, and permanently refusing a patient is an admin action.

entries.title: Health record and Results are easier to move around
entries.body: The record hub leads with your lists, keeps Add reachable on every screen size, and puts each record's actions inline where you are already looking.

entries.title: A flaky data source stops crying wolf
entries.body: A source that fails one hour and succeeds the next — a weather service having a bad afternoon — used to report itself as broken, badge and all, even though nothing was missing. It now says plainly that it is working with interruptions, and only escalates after three failures in a row or when nothing has arrived for a day. A source that does need attention is shown once, with its reason and all its actions together, and the run history groups repeated failures instead of alternating stripes.

entries.title: Settings housekeeping
entries.body: The AI provider and automation cards move to their own page under Server, which was carrying ten cards. The backup staleness alarm the health check reads is now editable instead of database-only, and a capability field that only ever had one option reads as plain text.

entries.title: Overdue safety follow-ups finally reach you
entries.body: A follow-up you tracked with a due date — the scan recommended in March — now sends a reminder when it goes overdue, and one more some weeks later, then stops. There is no new setting to find: recording the follow-up with a date is the ask, and the off switch is marking it done or saying you have decided against it, either of which ends it for good.

entries.title: As-needed dose limits can count milligrams, not just doses
entries.body: Because the safety counter groups the same ingredient across items, 200 mg and 800 mg ibuprofen were both simply "a dose" — so three prescription tablets read as calm while six low-dose ones tripped the limit. You can now record a milligrams-per-day maximum, and when every logged dose has a known amount the counter compares real exposure and says which basis it used.

entries.title: Fix a whole run of bad data at once
entries.body: A miscalibrated scale or an import that landed pounds as kilograms no longer means dozens of row-at-a-time edits. Data → Review grows a "Fix a run of data" panel: pick the field, source, and date range, preview every change (with a plain warning that corrected device rows stop receiving sync updates), then apply in one pass — with a 24-hour undo that restores values while leaving anything you edited afterwards alone. The Body weight chart links straight into it with "Fix a range".

entries.title: Workouts and food logging work offline
entries.body: The two gym-and-kitchen moments that still needed signal now queue like doses and weigh-ins: a workout session logged entirely offline is captured when you close the editor and syncs on reconnect (exactly once, sets and all), and the one-tap food serving and protein quick-adds queue too. Undo taps stay online-only — removing something you can't see the current total for would be a guess.

entries.title: Merging duplicate activities: pick any copy's value, per field
entries.body: When merging duplicate activities that genuinely disagree — say three copies with three distances — the conflict preview now lists every copy's value as a choice per field, pre-selected to the record you're keeping. Change the keeper and the preview re-orients. Works the same on the Review resolver and the Journal's multi-select merge.

entries.title: Patient portals is now a guided setup flow
entries.body: The portals page shows one step at a time — from "register your first portal" through mapping discovered patients to a steady-state status view — with a single next-step button instead of eight cards of forms. Everything else lives under a collapsed Manage section (where portals can now also be renamed), copy is shorter, and the page is narrower. Setup surfaces you've finished simply stop appearing.

entries.title: Nudges say things worth reading
entries.body: "With 0 days left" now reads "only today left" everywhere, praise skips generic session names instead of saying "Nice workout today", the workout nudge no longer states the same shortfall twice, limit-tier food groups sink to the end of the quick-log keyboard, the protein line drops its hedging, and a message that resolves itself now says what it was about ("Morning food log — handled in the app").

entries.title: Duplicate documents stop being re-uploaded forever, and logins can be named by email
entries.body: When the import tool offers a file whose records are already fully imported, allos now remembers that verdict and tells the tool not to send it again — and forgets automatically if you later delete the covering document, so nothing is ever silently skipped. Portal logins can now be named with an email address ("mom@gmail.com"); web addresses remain rejected everywhere. A migration applies automatically.

entries.title: One import, one count
entries.body: The import coverage card's "imported" number now always equals the document's extracted count. It previously missed medications, imaging, and several other domains, so the two numbers could disagree about the same import.

entries.title: Opening the desktop profile switcher no longer shoves the sidebar
entries.body: The switcher panel now drops over the sidebar's contents instead of pushing the navigation, calendar, and footer down by half a screen and snapping them back on close.

entries.title: A brand-new profile no longer opens on a wall of red "Overdue" screenings
entries.body: Screenings with no recorded history now show as a calm "No record yet — add a past date or schedule" setup list instead of red Overdue rows. Nothing about them is counted as late, badged, or sent as a reminder — real overdue states, backed by a recorded date, look exactly as before.

entries.title: The morning digest reports news, not plumbing
entries.body: Data-arrival lines now say what arrived ("Health Connect: steps, sleep, workouts") instead of meaningless raw row counts, and the weather cache no longer produces a permanent arrival line every single morning. Six smaller copy and grammar fixes ride along: no doubled "Today:" prefix, named overdue items instead of bare counts, merged supplement lines, and friendlier sleep phrasing.

entries.title: Energy and Calm from your daily check-in are now charted
entries.body: The check-in's energy and calm ratings each get the full treatment your mood rating already had: a Trends card, a tile, a detail page with history and corrections, and a star for the Overview grid. The calm chart plots the same high-is-calm scale the check-in card uses.

entries.title: Next-period forecasting and trying-to-conceive tracking
entries.body: The Cycle page (and a dashboard tile) now project your next period as a date window with an honest confidence label derived from your own cycle variability — never a bare date, never before three completed cycles, and paused entirely during pregnancy or after menopause. A new trying-to-conceive section records LH tests, waking temperature, and cervical mucus as ordinary observations and derives an evidence-based fertile window; it stays off until you turn it on.

entries.title: Pickers now lead with what you actually use
entries.body: The medication, supplement, brand, provider, and specialty pickers no longer open on the alphabet. Your own current medications and supplements come first, then a sensible common-choices list, then everything else A–Z — and the vaccine picker is now age-aware, leading with the doses that are plausibly next for this person instead of an infant schedule. Everything stays searchable; only the order changed.

entries.title: Trends now shows how consistent your wellness practices have been
entries.body: The Trends overview gained a Practices section: one cell per completed week showing whether each practice hit its weekly range, your sessions-per-week charted against the band you declared, and average session length for practices that record minutes. It's calm by design — an under-target week is a neutral cell, never a warning — and every card links back to Wellness.

entries.title: The food nudge keyboard can now be collapsed
entries.body: The Telegram food nudge's "Show more" now has a matching "Show less" that folds the keyboard back a page (never below the compact default), and the "More…" link that left the chat for the app is gone — the buttons are the whole flow. A keyboard you've expanded also stays the size you chose when the message later updates itself.

entries.title: One identity bar and one profile switcher, everywhere
entries.body: Multi-profile instances get a single identity bar — stacked avatars of the profiles in your view with the acting profile always first, ringed, and named. On a phone it replaces the wordmark in the top bar, so "whose data is this?" is answerable without opening anything; on desktop it sits at the top of the sidebar. Tapping it opens one switcher panel (a drawer from the top on phones, an expanding list on desktop) where each person has two separate controls: switch who you're acting as, or toggle them in and out of your view. The old bottom-of-sidebar profile menu and the view-strip banner are retired; "Signed in as" moved next to Log out, and the import-review count now badges the Data entry in navigation. Single-profile instances are unchanged.

entries.title: Documents and training goals delete cleanly again
entries.body: Deleting a document whose extracted medication an illness episode later stopped used to fail with a database error — the episode's stop record blocked it. Stop records now keep the medication's name as their own snapshot, so the episode still says what it stopped while the document deletes, reprocesses, and reassigns cleanly (a migration applies automatically). Deleting a training goal a protocol referenced was blocked the same way: the protocol now simply loses its adherence link and survives, matching how other areas already behave.

entries.title: Every digest category can now be tuned
entries.body: The morning digest's Tune control now covers all ten categories, including lab results and activities. Turning a category down only quiets its routine lines: a flagged lab result always comes through, and a training day that set a personal record still appears. The row copy states exactly what each toggle can never hide.

entries.title: One update notice per deploy
entries.body: A new deploy used to raise two separate notices — a banner at the top and a bar at the bottom, each with its own reload button, and taking one could re-offer the update you'd just taken. There is now a single "Update ready" notice that names what was deployed, and its reload always lands you on the new version with nothing re-offering it afterwards.

entries.title: Weekly targets you've been under for a month get a gentle right-size offer
entries.body: When a weekly goal — a wellness practice, a training routine, or a food habit — has been under its target for four straight completed weeks, its page now offers to lower the target to the pace you actually keep, or to stop tracking it while keeping every logged session. Nothing changes unless you tap it, substance limits are never touched, and the Telegram pace nudge carries the same one-tap offer only when it was already messaging you.

entries.title: Shared bottles and your items now exchange product details
entries.body: Creating a shared bottle from a supplement or medication carries over its name and strength instead of making you retype them, and the medicine cabinet gained "Add for another person": pick a household member and their add form opens pre-filled from the bottle and already linked to it. A bottle's strength and form now show wherever it appears, and editing the bottle updates every linked item's display automatically.

entries.title: The portal name list an import tool can fetch is scoped to your household
entries.body: The API endpoint that lets the document-import tool read portal and account names now returns only accounts claimed by people you can access, matching how portal sync reports were scoped earlier. Admins still see the full list, and a brand-new portal stays visible so setup keeps working.

entries.title: The pull-to-refresh icon no longer sits permanently on screen
entries.body: In the installed app, the pull-to-refresh indicator now fades out when you're not pulling and no refresh is running. It previously stayed fully visible at the top of the screen from the moment a page loaded.

entries.title: Portal sync problems stay within their own household
entries.body: The patient-portals status card could show another household's portal failure message — including its free-text error — to anyone with a login on the instance. Portal run reports are now scoped by reachability: you see failures only for portal accounts bound to profiles you can access (plus unplaced first-contact runs, for the people who manage those). Portal names in the shared registry remain instance-wide, as designed.

entries.title: One person on two portal logins no longer imports twice
entries.body: Portals regenerate their export files on every request, so the same records could arrive looking like brand-new documents — especially when one person is reachable through two portal logins — and every visit ended up recorded twice. Allos now recognizes a health-record file by the clinical entry ids inside it, not just its bytes: an offer whose records exactly match a document already held is refused as already imported, a portal sync's repeat offers land no rows at all, and partly-overlapping exports still store normally. Existing documents are recognized retroactively. Operators: migration 136 applies automatically.

entries.title: Telegram messages now correct themselves when things change in the app
entries.body: Take a dose in the app, and the Telegram reminder that offered a ✅ Taken button stops presenting it as outstanding: on the next hourly tick, every live message re-checks its buttons against what actually happened — resolved actions are stripped, fully handled messages close with an honest line, and yesterday's buttons never stay tappable into today. A confirmation from one family member's chat also corrects everyone else's copy. Silent and cheap by design: an unchanged message is never edited.

entries.title: One language for integration status, and a sync history that reads like a log
entries.body: A provider's status now looks the same everywhere — the Integrations grid, its setup page, and Data → Review speak one vocabulary (Connected, Partial sync, Sync failing, Needs reconnect) with one timestamp style and one accounting. The setup page becomes the provider's home with a proper history table: a reason on every failure row, no-op runs collapsed, and weather reported in forecast language (“Forecast refreshed · 16 readings revised”) instead of record counts. Review is now an inbox: only providers needing attention expand; healthy ones collapse to a line. The “What this wrote” drill-down also stops appearing on syncs that never record per-record detail.

entries.title: The morning digest now tells you what changed
entries.body: Out-of-range vitals, your daily check-in, new symptoms, and what synced overnight can now appear in the digest's New section — ranked so a flagged result always leads, capped so a busy day says “+2 more” instead of flooding. On favorable days a sunlight line names the window (“Sunny, UV moderate until 4pm”), and an optional daily step target adds a calm verdict for yesterday plus one quiet afternoon note when the day is well behind — counted, never escalated, and stale sync data stays silent rather than guessing.

entries.title: Lipid ratios computed for you — and a lighter Biomarkers page
entries.body: LDL/HDL and Cholesterol/HDL ratios now appear beside your labs even when the lab didn't print them, computed from the same draw and flagged against their reference bands. The Biomarkers browser also stops shipping your entire lab history to the browser on every visit: panels load their readings when you open them, so decades of results cost nothing until asked for.

entries.title: Pickers instead of blank boxes across ten medical forms
entries.body: Allergen, gene, condition, family-history, visit-type, care-plan, side-effect and activity fields now offer their real vocabularies as you type — with free text always allowed. This matters for safety: a recognized allergen or gene spelling is stored in the exact form the drug-allergy and pharmacogenomic cross-checks match on. Picking a condition by name now applies its ICD-10 code automatically, the way medication picks apply their RxNorm code, and the care-plan status picker says plainly which statuses keep nudging Upcoming and which stop.

entries.title: Tune your morning digest from the digest itself
entries.body: A ⚙️ Tune button on the digest expands in place into per-category toggles: turn a category down to notable-only and routine lines stop while anything important still comes through — an out-of-range reading, a notable mood shift, an unusual night's sleep. Flagged results can never be silenced, demoting everything makes the digest short but never gone, and the same toggles live in Settings → Notifications. In a household, no one's tap thins anyone else's digest.

entries.title: Deleted documents stay deleted — and portal syncs stop re-uploading what you already have
entries.body: The portal tool can now ask Allos what it already holds before sending anything, so daily syncs stop re-uploading megabytes and stop inflating the import feed with skipped rows — and a document that quietly went missing gets noticed and re-sent on the next run. Deleting a document now leaves a memory: an automated sync can never bring it back, a new “blocked from re-acquisition” list in Data → Review shows what's blocked with a one-tap Allow again, and re-uploading the file yourself also unblocks it. Operators: migration 134 applies automatically.

entries.title: Training, Longevity and Timeline pages do less work per visit
entries.body: Three heavy pages stopped repeating themselves: the Training overview no longer scans your whole strength history twice per view, the Longevity page no longer recomputes a heatmap for every experiment you've ever finished, and the Timeline evaluates its weather context once per page instead of once per day. Long histories load noticeably lighter; nothing changes in what's shown.

entries.title: Caregivers can view a family member's symptom photos and videos again
entries.body: Opening a household member's illness episode as a caregiver used to show the clip tiles but fail to play them. The media now follows the same access rules as the episode page itself: if you can see the episode, you can play its clips and photos. Access stays strictly grants-based, and every cross-profile view is recorded in the audit trail.

entries.title: Monday's workout suggestion remembers Saturday
entries.body: Next-workout focus now respects muscle recovery across the week boundary: big muscle groups rest a couple of days, small ones a day, and the least-recently-trained region leads. When everything you train is still fresh, the day is framed as a recovery day instead of forcing a pick — and when the week genuinely can't be met without today, the suggestion says both facts out loud (“Back was Saturday — 1/2 with today left.”). Phones also regain the Equipment door on the Training header.

entries.title: Your portal reminds the right person — and the tool learns its own config
entries.body: Allos now notices when a patient portal hasn't been checked in a while — or when someone just had an appointment and new results are likely waiting — and quietly asks the right person: the one whose login actually runs the portal tool, on their own Upcoming list and morning digest. A "Request sync" button covers the case where the person managing Allos isn't the person at the right computer. Asks expire on their own, are answered automatically by the next run (even a failed one — you went to the machine), and never escalate. And the portal tool can now fetch its own configuration from Allos — portal and login names, spelled exactly right — so a typo'd slug stops being a mystery refusal.

entries.title: Portal setup gets honest about its first run
entries.body: The very first portal sync no longer looks like nothing happened: the status line now says "The tool reported 3 patients — map them below to finish setup" instead of "No run reported yet." The tool can also report a portal-wide failure (a changed login page, a moved download) without inventing a patient, and the count of patients waiting to be mapped is now the number that are actually new. Plus a safety catch on mapping: the profile picker no longer preselects anyone, so a mis-click can't file a patient under whoever sorts first — and the show-once API token finally has a copy button.

entries.title: Patient portals grow up: household logins, discovered patients, and a truer name
entries.body: The portal integration is now "Patient portals" — MyChart was just the first door; any portal with a standard health-record export works the same way. Households with two portal logins get accounts ("Mom", "Dad"), so two patients who share a name on different logins can never collide onto one profile. The companion tool now reports the patient list it sees, and the card turns that into waiting-to-be-mapped entries any caregiver with write access can bind — or mark ignored for patients you don't want synced. Sync status shows per portal, per login, per patient.

entries.title: Documents remember which portal they came from
entries.body: A record uploaded through a portal now carries "Acquired via <portal>" in Data → Review and on the document itself. When two providers' portals disagree about an immunization, which copy came from where finally has an answer — and a hand-uploaded file says exactly that, by saying nothing.

entries.title: Portal mapping deletions are now properly fenced
entries.body: Removing a portal patient mapping now verifies you can write to the profile the mapping actually points at — resolved on the server, never trusted from the form. A crafted request can no longer delete another profile's mapping, and a concurrent re-bind makes the delete refuse rather than proceed on stale authority.

entries.title: Training that checks the forecast — without overruling you
entries.body: Outdoor suggestions now know the weather, and your tolerance is learned from your own history: if you ride at 3 °C, nothing parks your bike at 3 °C. In genuinely hostile conditions the suggestion swaps to a mapped indoor alternative and says exactly why — never a silent disappearance — and a parked activity no longer piles up 'staleness' pressure while it waits out the season. When good outdoor days are scarce, the morning digest and Upcoming name the week's best window for your ride. Logged outdoor sessions also carry a small conditions stamp ("31°C · clear"), so a slow run in the heat explains itself.

entries.title: Weather becomes context: heatwaves, pollen, and med-aware sun safety
entries.body: Allos now caches daily weather and air quality for your home location and derives five situations from it — heatwave, cold snap, pressure swing, high pollen, poor air quality. They behave like the situations you already use: an antihistamine keyed to high pollen comes due while the pollen holds, the digest mentions the conditions, and Trends can ask whether a pressure swing explains a rough night. And if a medication in your stack makes sun or heat riskier — a photosensitizing antibiotic, a diuretic in a heatwave — the day's safety note says so, quietly, on the surfaces you already read.

entries.title: Patient portals get real names — and syncs tell you whose data arrived
entries.body: If your health system's portal was swallowed by a merger (MyChart, we see you), Allos now keeps a registry of portals under Settings → Integrations, with each connected account mapped to the profile it feeds. Sync reports name the portal and the person, so a household with two MyChart logins can finally tell whose labs just landed. Identities Allos hasn't seen before are surfaced instead of guessed at — nothing is ever silently filed to the wrong person.

entries.title: Upload documents from anywhere — tokens, an API, and a tiny CLI
entries.body: You can now mint API tokens under Settings → Account & security: login-tied, scoped to document upload only, shown once, and revocable per device. With one, a new authenticated endpoint accepts document uploads from outside the browser — same ingest pipeline, same per-profile dedup, honest per-file results — and a dependency-free command-line script uploads a folder of files from any machine. Name a token per device so retiring one never disturbs the others.

entries.title: Nudges that read like they know you
entries.body: A sweep over every message the app sends. The protein line now says when you've reached your goal instead of implying a shortfall; the workout nudge leads with the exact target driving its suggestion; the daily digest previews today's recommended workout and drops its redundant tail on Telegram. A second same-day workout nudge acknowledges the session you already did, and if mood check-ins are about to auto-pause, the final reminder says so — pausing quietly unless you ask to keep them.

entries.title: The safety tier stops lying
entries.body: Missed-dose escalations now reach every channel you configured — Web Push and Home Assistant included, not just Telegram — and a broken safety channel finally shows up in delivery health. Escalations state how long a dose has been unconfirmed and offer a one-tap Skip. The /dose command shows the same redose safety verdicts as the app, push notifications stop asking you to tap buttons they can't show, a next-morning tap on yesterday's household round is refused instead of mislogged, and shared-chat messages always name whose dose they mean.

entries.title: Imaging saves show up reliably — and failures say so
entries.body: Adding an imaging study could occasionally leave the list unchanged even though the save landed, because the page's refresh path pointed at a redirect stub. Saves now repaint the imaging list directly, and a refused submission shows its error instead of silently rendering nothing.

entries.title: Biomarkers on your phone: results first
entries.body: On a phone, the Biomarkers page used to open with nearly 1,900 pixels of summary cards before the first actual panel of results. The panel index now leads — visible on the first screen — with the trajectory warning keeping its headline up top and folding its details, while the starred lens and bio-age cards follow whole below. Desktop is unchanged.

entries.title: Broken syncs finally speak up — and food taps count right
entries.body: A revoked or persistently failing integration used to sit quietly on-device while your data went stale. The morning digest now names each broken source with a link to fix it, and a connection that simply stopped syncing — recording nothing at all — raises its own attention item with per-provider staleness thresholds. Also fixed: tapping a Telegram food nudge outside its original window now counts toward the right meal, so the button's (n) tally matches what you actually logged.

entries.title: Journal search now searches your whole history
entries.body: Searching or filtering the training log used to look only at the days already loaded on screen — a matching workout from months ago simply didn't exist as far as the page knew. Search and every filter now query your entire ledger, paging over the matches themselves, with a new source filter and a fault count that reflects your whole history. An unfiltered journal loads exactly as fast as before.

entries.title: Cycle tracking stops lying to you — in both directions
entries.body: The "Period started today" quick action no longer confirms success when nothing was written — it tells you a period is already open, refuses an implausibly soon restart, and shows where you are in your cycle instead of offering the wrong button the moment a period ends. A one-tap "Still bleeding" reopens a just-ended period. And a forgotten "ended" tap no longer reads as menstrual forever: after ten days the app treats the period as probably over and asks you to set the end date — your record is never changed behind your back. New entries are checked for overlaps, future dates, and impossible ranges, with every refusal naming the conflict.

entries.title: Your half-entered workout survives anything
entries.body: Long forms now keep a local draft as you type: reload, crash, or a deploy mid-entry, and a banner offers your unsaved work back — Resume or Discard, your choice, never applied silently, always cleared once you actually save. Drafts stay on your device only and are wiped on logout. App updates also stopped yanking pages out from under you: a new version now waits with a small "Update ready" note, and you reload when you're ready — it even mentions if you have unsaved work open.

entries.title: A tidier supplement shelf and medicine cabinet
entries.body: The supplements page puts your working list back ahead of the safety reading, with a "More supplements" disclosure matching Food's. The medicine cabinet got a matching pass: profile-aware links back to each item, actions tucked into a standard overflow menu, and the usual delete confirmation. Linking a shared supply now confirms it worked and no longer lets a double-tap create duplicate bottles, and same-named linked items disambiguate by kind and dose so you always know which one you're looking at.

entries.title: Upcoming stops drowning you in routine
entries.body: The planning page's scheduled doses now fold into one line per band — "14 doses today · 9 taken" — expandable to the exact rows with their confirm buttons intact, and routine interaction/gene notes roll up the same way. Safety never folds: a missed-dose escalation or an as-needed limit warning always renders individually, above the fold, and allergy conflicts keep their place at the top. The genuinely attention-worthy items stop being needles in a haystack.

entries.title: File a document or log a practice without leaving where you are
entries.body: The quick-log sheet gains an Add document row that opens the familiar upload form in place — camera included, so photographing a paper result is one tap — and a Log practice row listing your tracked practices with this week's standing. The command palette learned both too: search for "scan" or "lab report" to file a document, or type "log sauna" to record a practice — a bare practice name stays a search, so you never log by accident.

entries.title: Weekly, alternating-day, and taper schedules — without giving up reminders
entries.body: Intake items can finally say when they actually happen: weekly (methotrexate, a GLP-1 shot), alternating days, every N days, or specific weekdays. A weekly medication now reminds and escalates on its day and stays silent the other six — no more choosing between daily nagging and demoting it to no reminders at all. Off-day quick-logs still work and ask an honest confirm; adherence math counts only the days a dose was actually owed.

entries.title: Charts you can actually read on a phone — and a day chart you can touch
entries.body: Chart text now has a real minimum: labels are sized against how small the chart can actually render, so nothing shrinks below legibility (two charts were quietly under the floor and got fixed). The day-at-a-glance chart labels your wake and bed times, names its activity blocks, and drops the machine-analysis tick marks. The intraday chart gained a touch layer: scrub for an exact heart-rate reading, drag or tap to zoom, all with the keyboard supported — and annotation labels now stay inside the plot instead of smearing past its edge.

entries.title: Search finally knows your whole record
entries.body: Global search and record Q&A now cover nine domains that were previously unsearchable: providers, imaging, genomics, dental, skin lesions, illness episodes, protocols, wellness practices, and equipment. Hits deep-link straight to the right detail page, providers only surface through your own records that name them, and asking a question can now cite any of these domains as evidence.

entries.title: Skin lesions and allergies join the visit trail
entries.body: The last two clinical observations without a visit link now have one: a skin lesion or an allergy can be tied to the encounter where it was noted, and an allergy can also record which provider confirmed it. They join the same link, suggestion, and unlink flow every other record type uses, and imported allergy records pick up their visit automatically when the document names one. Deleting a visit never deletes the observation — the record outlives the appointment.

entries.title: Trends opens on one page: your stars, then your body
entries.body: The Overview and Body tabs merged into a single landing surface: the trending digest up top, your starred cards in the order you arranged them, and the full body census streaming in below — now one flat ranked stack instead of titled boxes, so your stars and the everyday-first order decide what leads. Fitness, Nutrition, and Insights remain their own tabs. Old bookmarks to the Body tab land on the merged page, and the page arrives as fast as the old Overview tab did alone.

entries.title: The review inbox now tells you what to double-check
entries.body: Document extraction now reports how sure it was about each captured row. The import detail page gains a "Check these first" card that ranks the least-certain rows to the top with the model's stated reason, and Data → Review badges each document with how many rows deserve a look. Nothing is blocked or hidden by this — a document extracted before this feature simply shows no badge, and a row the model was confident about behaves exactly as before.

entries.title: Must, should, may: your supplements and meds now carry an honest obligation
entries.body: Priority levels and the separate as-needed flag collapse into one clear setting: must (missing it is an incident — reminders and escalation), should (reminded and counted, never escalated), and may (never pushed, no misses — it simply stays one tap away in its usual slot). Rarely-taken supplements get a gentle Demote offer on their own reminder, never a new notification; accepting moves them into a calm "available" shelf on Upcoming instead of deleting anything. Medications default to must, and lowering one spells out exactly what safety net you are giving up — while interaction, gene, and upper-limit warnings fire identically no matter the level. Daily digests now lead with what actually changed — notably missed and resumed — instead of a fraction.

entries.title: Wellness practices grow up: findable, editable, and safely deletable
entries.body: The Wellness page now shows up in navigation, recent pages, and the command palette. Practices gained the full lifecycle they were missing: cadence rules that refuse impossible values out loud, protection against two practices silently sharing one history, session editing, a shared history/progress/heatmap view, and — at last — the choice between stop tracking (keeps your history) and permanent deletion (with undo). Protocol pages were tightened alongside, and protocol outcomes now rank by which biomarkers actually have before-and-after data to show.

entries.title: All your scans, one source — and a strict mode that means it
